title: Designing a Notation for the Senses
research_question: To understand the role of non-visual senses in urban spaces and to design tools (a notation system) for crafting urban environments that respond to these other senses.

participants.description: Advisory board; groups of senior undergraduate and Masters students from architecture, urban design, product design, anthropology and sound design.
participants.recruitment: Not explicitly stated, implied as collaborators/testers within a research project.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Plan drawings of urban spaces, annotated with sensory notation symbols (radar diagrams, lines, descriptor words).
Urban environments (routes, static places like squares) where sensory observations were made and recorded using the notation.

measures.instrument: Radar diagram method with descriptor terms for Visual, Aural, Tactile, Kinetic, Thermal, Chemical senses, priority ranking, corroboration, temporality.

findings.antecedent: Lefebvre's theory of rhythm, incorporating bodily rhythms (heart rate, breathing) into the notation process
findings.consequent: phenomenological basis of the notation system
findings.mechanism: The phenomenological basis of the work is clear, to the point of incorporating one’s own bodily rhythms into the process: an awareness of the heart rate and pumping of blood around the body, the action of breathing.
findings.quote: The phenomenological basis of the work is clear, to the point of incorporating one’s own bodily rhythms into the process

findings.antecedent: Initial matrix notation for senses (based on Laban and Lynch symbols)
findings.consequent: Advisory board reactions to the notation system
findings.mechanism: Valuable lessons were learned through this process of design and testing, however, that lead to the development of the subsequent system.
findings.quote: This notation was tested with our advisory board, and met with mixed reactions. Valuable lessons were learned through this process

mechanisms: The notation system aims to allow for creative replication through a common code or rudimentary language, facilitating understanding and recording phenomenological experiences, and establishing patterns for new design solutions.
The notation incorporates bodily rhythms (heart rate, breathing) to ground the phenomenological basis of sensory experience.
implementation_implications: The developed Sensory Notation method and Pattern Book can be used to create a design guide to encourage multi-modality in urban design.
The notation can be used to record existing sites, diagnose problems, or describe desirable places for new constructions.
The system aims to produce 'scores for the senses' that allow for creative replication and pattern identification for urban design.

tables.description: Gibson’s perceptual systems chart, outlining Name, Mode of Attention, Receptive Units, Anatomy of the Organ, Activity of the Organ, Stimuli Available, and External Information Obtained for basic orienting, auditory, haptic, taste-smell, and visual systems.
Descriptor terms for Visual, Aural, Tactile, Kinetic, Thermal, and Chemical senses (e.g., Dark, High Pitch, Static, Strong, Hot, Weak).

limitations: Audio recording technologies do not fully replicate all effects of aural perception, such as memory or attention functions (e.g., Cocktail Party effect).
The initial matrix notation received mixed reactions from the advisory board, indicating areas for further development.
The taxonomy of senses, while useful for systematization, is an 'artifice' that divides the sensorium, which is experienced as a totality with corroboration and overlapping between senses.

paper_metadata.title: Movement and the Rubber Hand Illusion
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Movement and the Rubber Hand Illusion
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: When a participant views a rubber hand being stroked by a paintbrush while his/her real hand is unseen and similarly stroked by another paintbrush, a misperception known as the rubber hand illusion occurs whereby tactile sensations are falsely referred to the non-body part. The purpose of the current study was to further examine the rubber hand illusion with conditions of movement. An apparatus was devised that would synchronise visual with felt movement in an active condition and a passive condition. An asynchronous condition was included as a control in which visual and felt movement were purposely disconnected. The three movement conditions (active, passive, and asynchronous) were statistically compared in order to assess our prediction that synchronous conditions of movement (especially active) would generate more reports of the illusion. The performance of the movement conditions was evaluated against a visual-tactile condition, which is a known contributor to the rubber hand illusion. Not only significantly more robust reports of the illusion were obtained when visual movement and felt movement were synchronised but there was also a trend toward stronger reports in the active condition rather than the passive condition. Interestingly, the pattern of results differed according to the particular question on the self-report.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: The paper extends Lefebvre's theory of rhythm by incorporating its concepts, particularly bodily rhythms (e.g., heart rate, breathing), as a foundational framework for designing a notation system that represents the temporal and experiential aspects of sensory phenomena.
The notation system is developed with a phenomenological basis, aiming to capture and represent subjective, lived sensory experiences rather than purely objective physical properties.

stimulus_images.description: Diagrams and examples illustrating the proposed notation system for sensory experiences, including its symbols, structure, and application.
